1. The image shows a grid of monthly squares running from January 1991 to July 2016. Each square is a month in which someone could have bought a home. A lit (light) square means the buyer came out ahead after ten years. A dark square means the renter came out ahead. The frames cite FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. They are labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. Very little changes across the six frames. The grid stays the same. The one visible change is that a caption appears in frames 4 to 6: "2002 to 2007: 6 of 72 (8.3%)". A highlighted orange column and a bright strip of squares in the middle of the grid seem to mark that 2002–2007 window. Most of the early squares are light and most of the later squares are dark.

3. Whether buying beat renting depended heavily on when you bought. Buying in the early 1990s mostly paid off over ten years. Buying around 2002–2007 rarely did: only 6 of those 72 months, or 8.3%, favored the buyer. Those buyers faced the housing crash. So the grid shows a mixed historical record rather than one answer, and the outcome depended on timing.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that buying is not automatically cheaper than renting, and that the starting date matters a lot. That is my reading of the picture, not something it states.

5. Advice: none stated on screen. The inference in item 4 is my own conclusion. The only text is the labels, the legend, the date range, the 6-of-72 caption and the disclaimer "history, not a forecast", which actually warns against drawing forward-looking advice.
